title: Max Dot Product of Two Subsequences
description: Brute force to optimized: enumerating every equal-length subsequence pair versus a 2D DP table combining Kadane's diagonal recurrence with skip transitions.

content.title: Max Dot Product of Two Subsequences

blocks.text: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, return the maximum dot product achievable between a non-empty subsequence of nums1 and a non-empty subsequence of nums2 of the SAME length (a subsequence may skip elements, but must preserve their original relative order).

blocks.caption: A 2D DP table pairs up elements from both arrays, extending, restarting, or skipping as needed

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Looking for the best pairing between two SUBSEQUENCES (order preserved, gaps allowed)","A 2D DP table over positions in both arrays, similar in shape to Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray, but allowing SKIPS"],["Pairing two elements only helps if it extends a currently-positive running product streak","Kadane's \"extend if positive, else restart fresh\" idea, applied along the DP table's diagonal"],["Either array's current element could simply be skipped, not just matched","Unlike Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray's hard reset on a mismatch, this DP also considers dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] (skipping one element entirely)"]]}

blocks.text: Given nums1 and nums2, choose a non-empty subsequence from each, of the same length, pairing them up in order, to maximize the sum of the pairwise products (the dot product).

blocks.title: Analogy: Best Matching Investments Across Two Timelines
blocks.text: Like having two timelines of possible investment returns (some positive, some negative), and being allowed to pick any number of matching investment PAIRS (one from each timeline, in the same relative order, though not necessarily adjacent), multiplying each matched pair's returns together and summing the results. A pair is only worth including if the running total it would extend is positive; otherwise, it's better to start counting fresh from that pair, or skip one side's element entirely and look elsewhere.

blocks.caption: Every cell either extends a positive diagonal streak, restarts fresh, or inherits from skipping one element

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Choosing nums1 = [2,-2] (indices 0,2) and nums2 = [3,-6] (indices 0,2): dot product = 2*3 + (-2)*(-6) = 6 + 12 = 18","Dot product: 18","This pairing, skipping index 1 in both arrays, achieves the maximum"],["Answer","18","No other pairing of equal-length subsequences achieves a higher dot product"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Every possible pairing gives a negative product (since one array is all negative, the other all positive)","Best single-pair dot product: -1","Since a non-empty subsequence is required, the least-bad single pairing must be chosen"],["Answer","-1","No pairing can achieve a non-negative result here, so the smallest-magnitude negative product is the best achievable"]]}

blocks.text: Before enumerating every possible pair of equal-length subsequences, notice this closely resembles Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray's 2D table, but with two key differences: elements are multiplied (not just matched), and skipping an element (not just a hard reset) is always an option.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Define dp[i][j] as the best dot product achievable using SOME non-empty matching between nums1[:i] and nums2[:j] (not necessarily using nums1[i-1] or nums2[j-1] at all).

Observation 2: Pairing nums1[i-1] with nums2[j-1] contributes their product; this pairing either extends a previous positive streak ending at dp[i-1][j-1], or (if that streak wasn't positive) starts a fresh streak using just this one pair.

Observation 3: Alternatively, this cell could simply INHERIT the best result from ignoring nums1[i-1] (dp[i-1][j]) or ignoring nums2[j-1] (dp[i][j-1]), since a subsequence is free to skip elements entirely, unlike a contiguous subarray.

Observation 4: dp[i][j] is the maximum of these options: (max(dp[i-1][j-1], 0) + product) or dp[i-1][j] or dp[i][j-1]. The final answer is simply dp[n][m].

Recognizing this as "Kadane's extend-or-restart logic, applied on a 2D grid, PLUS the option to skip either array's current element entirely" reuses two already-familiar ideas together.

This is a 2D DP generalization combining Kadane's Algorithm's "extend if positive, else restart" recurrence with the "skip an element from either side" option seen in classic Longest Common Subsequence-style DP.
Enumerate every possible pair of equal-length subsequences (one from each array), compute each pairing's dot product directly, and track the maximum.

items: Enumerate every possible subset (subsequence) of nums1 and every possible subset of nums2 that have matching lengths.
For each matching-length pair of subsequences, compute their dot product by pairing corresponding positions, and track the maximum found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible subset of each array is enumerated using bitmasks, since a subsequence corresponds exactly to some subset of positions, preserved in order.
Only subset pairs with EQUAL sizes are considered, since the problem requires matching-length subsequences.
The dot product is computed directly by pairing up the chosen elements in their original relative order.

blocks.text: Every possible pair of equal-length subsequences is checked directly, so the correct maximum dot product is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2^n * 2^m) in the worst case, from enumerating every subset of both arrays.
Space: O(n + m) for storing a single subset pair at a time.

Limitation: enumerating every possible subsequence pair directly ignores that the best pairing ending at any specific pair of positions depends only on a small, fixed set of neighboring DP states (the diagonal predecessor, and the two adjacent "skip" states).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force enumerates every possible subsequence pair directly, which is exponential. Instead, build a 2D DP table where dp[i][j] represents the best dot product achievable using some non-empty matching within nums1[:i] and nums2[:j]. Fill it using three possible sources per cell: extending a positive diagonal predecessor (or starting fresh) by pairing the current elements, or inheriting from skipping either array's current element entirely. The final answer is simply dp[n][m].

Initialize a (n+1) by (m+1) table to negative infinity. For each cell (i, j) from 1 to n and 1 to m, compute the product of nums1[i-1] and nums2[j-1], then set dp[i][j] to the maximum of: (max(dp[i-1][j-1], 0) + product), dp[i-1][j], and dp[i][j-1].
Fill a 2D DP table where each cell extends a positive diagonal streak, restarts fresh, or inherits from skipping an element.

blocks.title: Reading the table
blocks.text: dp[3][3] reaches 18 by extending the positive streak dp[2][2]=6 with the product (-2)*(-6)=12, giving 6+12=18. dp[4][3] then inherits this same value (18) from dp[3][3], since pairing nums1[3]=5 with nums2[2]=-6 would only hurt (5*-6=-30). The final answer, dp[4][3], is 18, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m), a single pass filling every cell of the table exactly once.
Space: O(n * m) for the table (reducible to O(m) using a rolling row).

Every optimal matching either uses the pairing (nums1[i-1], nums2[j-1]) -- in which case it either extends a previous positive streak (dp[i-1][j-1], if beneficial) or starts a completely fresh streak using just this pair -- or it doesn't use one of these two elements at all, in which case the best result is already captured by dp[i-1][j] or dp[i][j-1]. Taking the maximum across all these possibilities at every cell guarantees the globally optimal matching is found by the time the table is complete.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["dp[i-1][j-1] > 0","Extend that positive streak by adding the current pair's product"],["dp[i-1][j-1] <= 0 (or undefined)","Start a fresh streak using just the current pair's product alone"],["Skipping nums1[i-1] or nums2[j-1] entirely is better","Inherit from dp[i-1][j] or dp[i][j-1] instead"]]}

items: dp is initialized to negative infinity everywhere, since a "non-empty" matching hasn't been established yet at any cell before it's computed.
max(dp[i-1][j-1], 0) is the crucial Kadane's-style adjustment: only carry forward a PRIOR streak if it was actually positive, otherwise treat it as 0 (starting fresh).

The final answer, dp[n][m], represents the best matching using the FULL extent of both arrays (with the flexibility to have skipped any prefix elements along the way, already baked into the recurrence).

blocks.text: This problem combines Kadane's "extend if positive, else restart" recurrence (applied diagonally, as in Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray) with the additional flexibility of skipping either array's current element entirely, since subsequences (unlike subarrays) allow gaps.

items: Forgetting the dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] skip options, which would incorrectly force every chosen position in nums1 to align with some position in nums2 with no ability to skip.
Forgetting to clamp the diagonal predecessor at 0 before adding the current product, which would incorrectly carry forward a harmful negative streak.

Confusing this with Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray's hard reset-to-zero on a mismatch; here, a "mismatch" doesn't reset anything, since any product (positive or negative) can still be chosen, just weighed against skipping.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Both arrays are entirely negative and entirely positive respectively (or vice versa)","The answer is the least-negative single-pair product, since a non-empty subsequence is mandatory"],["nums1 or nums2 has only 1 element","The best matching can only ever use exactly 1 pair, whichever single pairing in the other array's elements is largest"],["Both arrays are identical and entirely positive","The answer is achieved by matching every element with itself in order, summing all squared values"]]}

items: Explicitly connect this problem to both Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray (the 2D diagonal DP shape) and Kadane's Algorithm (the extend-if-positive-else-restart logic), while clearly flagging the "skip" option as the one crucial addition, since recognizing which parts are reused versus which part is new demonstrates precise understanding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximum dot product / matching sum between two SUBSEQUENCES (not subarrays) of possibly different signs" points toward a 2D DP table combining Kadane's extend-or-restart logic on the diagonal with explicit skip transitions from both the row above and the column to the left.

items: How would you also report the actual chosen pairs, not just the dot product? Track back-pointers at each cell indicating whether it came from extending, restarting, or one of the two skip transitions, then walk backward from dp[n][m].

How does this differ from Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray? That problem requires elements to MATCH exactly and resets hard to 0 on any mismatch; this problem multiplies elements regardless of value and never hard-resets, since any product can be chosen or skipped as beneficial.

What if the subsequences were required to be contiguous (subarrays) instead? This becomes a much simpler 1D sliding-window-style problem, since contiguous subarrays of the same length starting at fixed offsets could be checked with simple running products, no 2D DP needed.

A 2D DP combining the diagonal extend-or-reset recurrence from Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray with Kadane's Algorithm's "reset when the running value goes non-positive" philosophy, plus explicit row/column skip transitions characteristic of Longest Common Subsequence-style DP.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(2^n * 2^m) time, O(n + m) space.
Optimized (2D DP table): O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space.

items: Pattern: 2D DP table combining Kadane's "extend if positive, else restart" diagonal recurrence with explicit skip transitions
Core Idea: Each cell either extends a positive diagonal streak with the current pair's product, starts fresh, or inherits from skipping either array's current element
Time: O(n * m)
Space: O(n * m), reducible to O(m)

Most Important Observation: Unlike contiguous-subarray matching, subsequences allow skipping elements entirely, requiring explicit row/column inheritance transitions alongside the diagonal Kadane's-style recurrence
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: dp[i][j] = max(max(dp[i-1][j-1],0) + product, dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
